PHSCS 587

Double-gate electrostatics

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a symmetric gate pair controls the potential in a thin silicon body

A thin double-gate device places gate control on opposite sides of the silicon. This can reduce source/drain penetration, allow lower channel doping and make the full body participate in weak-inversion conduction. The exact charge distribution changes with bias.

For the reading’s symmetric dielectric-matched model, eigenlengths satisfy tan(πtox/λ)tan[πtsi/(2λ)] = εox/εsi. The associated longitudinal mode contains sinh(πy/λ). Physical oxide and body thickness matter; increasing dielectric constant does not eliminate all geometric length limits.

More gate-controlled channel can increase both current and intrinsic gate charge. In a thought experiment with two identical independent channels, doubling current also doubles intrinsic capacitance, so CV/I does not automatically improve. Actual advantages require comparing electrostatics, geometry, capacitance and drive together.

Example

For two ideal parallel copies of a channel, suppose each supplies 40 μA with 2 fF intrinsic load at a 0.8 V swing. One gives CV/I ≈ 40 ps; two give 4 fF and 80 μA, still about 40 ps before extrinsic effects.

Practice

1. Why can a double-gate structure be valuable even without a twofold intrinsic delay improvement?

Separate short-channel electrostatic control from merely adding a parallel channel.

It can suppress contact influence, permit thinner controlled bodies and reduce reliance on high channel doping. Those benefits can enable a different operating design even when added charge accompanies added current.
